title: Controlled regeneration of complex organs in the adult body

concept.text: Conceptual synthesis: This innovation would enable a damaged adult organ to rebuild substantial lost tissue inside the body and recover useful function. It would require control over which cells multiply, what specialized cells they become, where they organize, and when growth stops. The intended outcome is functional tissue integrated with the existing organ, including the blood supply, nerve connections, and architecture needed for that organ’s work.

Scope synthesis: A convincing achievement could begin with substantial regeneration within one complex adult organ; it need not begin with regrowing an entire organ or limb. Rebuilding a whole heart, kidney, limb, or spinal cord would each be a separate, more demanding claim. A mechanism that works in one tissue would not by itself establish a general regenerative platform.

significance.text: Conditional significance: If regeneration restored enough functional tissue safely and durably, it could allow some damaged organs to recover without transplantation or permanent mechanical replacement. The revolutionary consequence would be a change from replacing an organ or compensating for its loss to rebuilding its biological capacity in place. This consequence depends on the amount, quality, and durability of restoration in each demonstrated indication.

Conditional downstream possibilities: Successful treatments could reduce reliance on replacement organs and devices in the conditions they actually treat. Broader benefits would depend on clinical eligibility, treatment timing, delivery, affordability, and whether the underlying disease continues to damage the regenerated tissue. Restoring part of an organ would not necessarily eliminate the need for other treatment.

Limits of the analogy: Regenerative ability in a neonatal animal, even if established, would provide biological motivation rather than a direct demonstration of safe regeneration in an adult human. Likewise, substantial tissue repair, whole-organ regeneration, and limb regeneration are different levels of achievement. None warrants assuming that a single regenerative switch can rebuild every organ.

missing_breakthrough.text: Research-problem synthesis: The missing capability is coordinated, controllable rebuilding of substantial functional tissue within an adult organ. The candidate identifies several linked requirements: sufficient cell proliferation, appropriate specialization, vascularization, innervation where needed, correct tissue architecture, and reliable termination of growth. These are a coherent engineering problem formulation; their detailed scientific scope is not verified by the retained source material.

Research-problem synthesis: Increasing cell number alone would not satisfy the goal. Newly formed tissue would need to survive, organize, connect to the remaining organ, and contribute to its function. The process would also need to avoid cancer, damaging fibrosis, and excessive or misplaced growth. Demonstrating benefit therefore requires evidence about both the regenerated tissue and the behavior of the organ as a whole.

Open mechanistic question: Whether one master pathway could coordinate these tasks across distinct organs remains unresolved in the supplied material. A shared growth signal would still need to produce the correct cell types, spatial organization, connections, and stopping behavior in each setting. Organ-specific control strategies may be necessary; the inputs do not establish which approach will succeed or whether these barriers remain unsolved in every relevant field today.

current_state.text: The supplied research reports that neonatal mammalian hearts can regenerate after certain injuries, with a reported window during the first two days of life, while adult heart regeneration remains severely limited. It attributes this account to a review identified as Neonatal Heart Regeneration: Comprehensive Literature Review, dated 2019, with DOI 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.118.033648. These are reported findings and bibliographic details from the inputs, rather than independently verified scientific content.

The evidence review found that the retained copy of the cited PubMed page contained only a cookie-access notice. It could therefore verify neither the document’s identity and authorship nor its abstract, full text, injury conditions, or neonatal regeneration window. The source index records a saved artifact, but saving the page did not provide inspectable scientific content. This access limitation prevents confirmation from the supplied copy; it does not establish that the reported findings are false.

Assessment boundary: The supplied evidence does not establish a safe adult-human organ-regeneration treatment. Even confirmation of the reported neonatal findings would not establish that capability. The review’s freshness record contains no search results supporting an assessment through November 1, 2026, and the recorded retrieval on November 11, 2026, supplies no scientific update. Accordingly, this record cannot determine the latest achievements, the present scope of adult regeneration, or whether particular barriers have since been overcome.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Controlled clinical studies should show durable regeneration of substantial lost tissue and meaningful restoration of function in at least one complex adult human organ. Evidence should establish both that tissue was rebuilt and that it contributes to organ function, rather than relying on a change in tissue volume or symptoms alone. These are proposed criteria for evaluating the innovation, not established standards from the cited source.
completion_criteria.label: Substantial adult human organ tissue regeneration durably restores function

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement and safety boundaries: Each indication should define in advance what counts as substantial tissue restoration, meaningful functional benefit, and acceptable risk. Follow-up over years should assess durability, cancer, fibrosis, abnormal growth, and deterioration of the rebuilt tissue. The appropriate duration and acceptable event rates remain to be specified; the supplied material supports no universal numerical thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined indication-specific success and risk criteria guide years-long safety follow-up

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope: Results should be reproducible across patients and independent clinical teams, with clear boundaries for eligible injuries, disease states, treatment timing, and organ condition. A general-platform claim would require convincing results in distinct organ systems, while whole-organ or limb regeneration would require direct evidence at that scale. A finite set of successful studies would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent clinical teams reproduce patient outcomes within clearly stated limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: BME-01, Manufacturing transplantable human organs on demand, and BME-12, Reliable, scalable animal-to-human organ transplantation, pursue replacement organs. BME-06, Long-term banking of transplantable human organs, concerns preserving organs for transplantation. BME-13, Durable autonomous artificial-organ replacement, pursues an engineered substitute. BME-11 instead seeks to restore biological tissue within the damaged adult organ. These approaches may serve overlapping needs while remaining distinct innovations.

Roster-based comparison: BME-17, Minimally invasive assembly of functional tissue inside the body, has especially close overlap because both concern functional tissue formed in the body. The distinction suggested by the titles is assembly of tissue versus controlled regeneration of a damaged organ. A future treatment could combine these approaches, but success at tissue assembly would still need evidence of organ restoration to satisfy BME-11.

Roster-based comparison: BME-03, Reconstruction of a chronically severed spinal cord, overlaps if regeneration restores spinal cord tissue and function after chronic severing. Its supplied title establishes a specific injury target, but does not establish its methods or full scope. BME-04, A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation, concerns an interface that could support function without necessarily regenerating the underlying tissue. BME-16, Long-lived tissue-integrated interfaces for implants, concerns durable implant integration. These entries should remain separate from organ regeneration.

Roster-based comparison: BME-02, Programmable delivery of genetic therapies to most tissues, could supply delivery capabilities for regenerative interventions. BME-05, Programmable living medicines that sense and respond inside the body, could overlap with control of a regenerative response. BME-08, Reliable, antigen-specific immune tolerance, could be relevant where an intervention requires a particular immune response. These are possible enabling relationships inferred from the roster titles; none independently demonstrates controlled organ rebuilding.

Roster-based comparison: BME-10, Validated patient-specific models for testing treatments before use, could help evaluate regenerative strategies. BME-15, Accessible deep-body molecular imaging, and BME-18, Long-lived continuous sensing of multiple clinically useful biomarkers, could help observe treatment response. BME-07, A broadly effective early-warning test for lethal cancers, has a potential safety connection because cancer is among the candidate’s stated concerns. Prediction, observation, and cancer detection remain distinct from controlling regeneration.

Roster-based comparison: BME-09, Physiological extra-uterine support through extreme prematurity, concerns developmental support rather than restoration of a damaged adult organ. BME-14, Shelf-stable, broadly compatible replacement for critical blood functions, concerns replacement of selected blood functions. These address different biomedical goals and do not establish regeneration of adult organ tissue.

unresolved_issues: The cited document’s identity, authorship, publication details, abstract, and full text remain unverified from the retained artifact.
The reported neonatal regeneration window, injury conditions, and limitations of adult heart regeneration require inspectable scientific evidence.
The latest research and clinical status cannot be assessed from the empty freshness record.
The feasibility of coordinating regeneration across distinct organs through a shared pathway remains unresolved.
Substantial tissue restoration, meaningful functional benefit, acceptable safety, and follow-up duration need indication-specific definitions.
Related-concept comparisons are limited to the supplied roster titles; detailed technical boundaries and possible combined approaches remain unspecified.

brief.title: Helping damaged organs rebuild themselves
possible: People with a damaged organ could recover some of its lost function by growing replacement tissue inside their own body. The new tissue would become a working part of the organ, with the blood supply, connections and structure it needs.
Success could begin with rebuilding a substantial part of an organ. It would not require regrowing a whole heart, kidney or limb.
why: For patients whose organs could be repaired this way, treatment could reduce reliance on transplants and permanent replacement devices. It would restore biological capacity where tissue was lost.

sources.who: Nicholas T. Lam and Hesham A. Sadek
sources.showed: Their review found that newborn mammal hearts can regenerate after some injuries through multiplication of existing heart muscle cells. The response depends on the injury and how it is performed.
sources.quote:
Both apical resection and ischemic infarction
injury in neonatal mice result in a robust regenerative response, mediated
by cardiomyocyte proliferation.
sources.cited_for: Newborn mammal hearts provide a biological example of rebuilding lost heart muscle.
sources.not_established: Regeneration in newborn animals does not establish safe regeneration in adult humans.

sources.who: Li Tang, Todd R. Heallen and colleagues
sources.showed: A gene therapy that weakened a brake on cell multiplication improved heart pumping in pigs after a heart attack. Treated hearts also showed evidence of heart muscle cell division and smaller scars.
sources.quote: exhibited a 14.3% improvement in ejection fraction (a measure of left ventricular systolic function), evidence of cardiomyocyte division, and reduced scar sizes compared to pigs receiving AAV9-GFP.
sources.cited_for: Stimulating tissue renewal can improve the function of an injured pig heart.
sources.not_established: The pig results do not establish durable benefit or safety in adult humans.

sources.who: Khatia Gabisonia, Fabio A. Recchia, Mauro Giacca and colleagues
sources.showed: A treatment using microRNA, a small molecule that regulates gene activity, improved pig heart pumping and reduced scars. Persistent activity later caused fatal heart rhythm disturbances in most treated pigs.
sources.quote:
At longer follow-up, however, persistent and uncontrolled 
expression of the microRNA resulted in sudden arrhythmic death of most of the treated pigs.
sources.cited_for: Early functional recovery can coexist with lethal consequences from uncontrolled growth signals.
sources.not_established: The treatment did not achieve safe, controlled repair.

sources.who: Gia Burjanadze, Fabio A. Recchia, Mauro Giacca and colleagues
sources.showed: Delaying the microRNA treatment after a heart attack produced no significant improvement in pig heart pumping or scar mass. Most treated pigs still died suddenly.
sources.quote:
Scar mass and cardiac contractile performance parameters were not signi ﬁcantly different between
AAV6-miR-199a–treated and AAV6-control pigs.
sources.cited_for: Treatment timing can determine whether a growth signal produces repair.
sources.not_established: The delayed treatment did not repair established injury safely.

sources.who: Agnieska Brazovskaja, Tomás Gomes and colleagues
sources.showed: Researchers mapped cells and tissue structure in human livers growing after a procedure that redirects blood flow. Samples from six patients revealed changes in cell activity, composition and organization.
sources.quote:
The data reveal changes to cell type pro-
portions, hepatocyte zonation, and intercellular communication in the
affected human liver.
sources.cited_for: Human liver regeneration involves changes in several cell types and tissue organization.
sources.not_established: Mapping liver regrowth does not establish controlled restoration of lost function in other damaged organs.

shown: Tang and colleagues have linked tissue renewal with improved pumping in injured pig hearts. Brazovskaja and colleagues have mapped how human liver tissue changes as it grows after blood flow is redirected. These are steps toward controlling repair, with different results in different organs.
missing: Controlled clinical studies have yet to demonstrate substantial rebuilding that durably restores function in a complex adult human organ.
New tissue must reliably form the right cells, structure, blood supply and necessary nerve connections, and contribute to the organ’s work.
Growth must stop reliably without cancer, harmful scarring or misplaced tissue.
Independent clinical teams must reproduce benefits within clearly defined patient and treatment limits.

milestones.label: Rebuilt adult human tissue durably restores organ function
milestones.explanation: Controlled clinical studies would have to show substantial tissue rebuilding and lasting functional recovery in a complex adult human organ. This would establish that the new tissue does useful work.

milestones.label: Defined success and risk criteria guide years of follow-up
milestones.explanation: Each condition would need predefined benefit and risk criteria, with years of follow-up for durability, cancer, scarring and abnormal growth. This would establish whether recovery lasts safely.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce outcomes within defined limits
milestones.explanation: Independent clinical teams would have to reproduce patient outcomes within stated treatment limits. Success across distinct organs would support broader use; whole-organ or limb regrowth would need direct evidence.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether a shared control pathway can coordinate repair across organs or each organ needs its own approach.
The amount of rebuilding, functional benefit and acceptable risk must be defined separately for each condition.
The follow-up needed to judge lasting benefit and delayed harm remains to be determined.

page.title: In situ regeneration of adult organs
page.definition: A treatment restores function in an adult organ with insufficient spontaneous recovery by directing new tissue formation within that organ. New cells acquire the required identities, integrate with the remaining tissue and blood supply, and stop proliferating after repair.

goal.need: Nearly 6.7 million US adults aged 20 years or older have heart failure. NIDDK reports that more than 808,000 people in the United States live with end-stage kidney disease. Regenerative treatments seek to recover native-organ function by rebuilding tissue in patients whose organs otherwise remain damaged.

completion.title: An adult-organ regeneration treatment receives FDA approval supported by tissue and functional recovery.
completion.criterion: At least one treatment receives traditional FDA marketing approval for an adult indication involving regeneration within the damaged native organ. Clinical evidence establishes new organ-specific tissue formation, integration and functional benefit. Growth resolves after repair, and efficacy persists through the indication-specific follow-up, with risks acceptable under the approved benefit–risk assessment. The functional efficacy evidence meets FDA's substantial-evidence standard.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, proposed boundary combining adult-human tissue regeneration with FDA traditional marketing approval.
completion.basis: FDA and EMA regenerative-product guidance, ISSCR translation guidelines, NIH programme goals and organ-regeneration prize and roadmap targets yielded no published cross-organ completion test. This proposed test combines the stated tissue-regeneration goal with FDA's clinical approval standard. The scope covers insufficient spontaneous recovery. Portal-vein embolization already induces human liver growth, documented in six patients in the 2024 liver atlas.

milestones.title: An organ-regeneration treatment establishes biological plausibility in a preclinical model.
milestones.criterion: Preclinical studies establish biological plausibility, biological activity and a dose range for an organ-regeneration treatment. In Tang et al. (2021), ejection fraction changed by +8.0 ± 0.5 percentage points in 3 high-dose treated pigs and −6.3 ± 1.9 in 7 controls during a 90-day study. One control was euthanized earlier. Values are mean ± SEM. Cardiomyocyte division was observed in these juvenile pigs. In Zwirner et al. (2024), 120-hour survival after 85% liver resection was 4/6 with pretreatment, 5/6 with treatment after surgery and 1/6 with vehicle.
milestones.set_by: FDA, November 2013 preclinical guidance, sections III.A and III.B.4, written for cellular and gene therapies.

milestones.title: An organ-regeneration treatment establishes preclinical safety for its intended clinical route.
milestones.criterion: Definitive preclinical studies establish reasonable safety of the proposed clinical route and characterize local and systemic toxicity, including delayed effects and dose dependence. In Gabisonia et al. (2019), sustained miR-199a expression improved pig-heart structure and function at 4 weeks, but 7/10 treated pigs followed longer died suddenly at weeks 7–8. The result identifies a dose-and-duration control problem for that intervention.
milestones.set_by: FDA, November 2013 preclinical guidance, sections III.A and III.B.5, written for cellular and gene therapies.
milestones.threshold_quote: Establishment of feasibility and reasonable safety of the investigational product’s proposed clinical route of administration (ROA).

milestones.title: An organ-regeneration treatment is administered to people in a phase 1 investigation.
milestones.criterion: An investigational organ-regeneration treatment enters human dosing under a phase 1 protocol assessing pharmacological effects and dose-associated adverse effects. On 11 November 2025, Medley reported dosing 3 adults with ischemic heart failure in SALVADOR-HF and safety-review permission to escalate YAP101 dosing. This developer result was not peer reviewed. The 2024 HRX215 paper reports 36 healthy men receiving the liver-regeneration drug and 12 receiving placebo, with no severe or serious adverse events.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: An organ-regeneration treatment produces preliminary evidence of effectiveness in patients.
milestones.criterion: Phase 2 studies evaluate effectiveness for a specified indication and common short-term risks, producing preliminary evidence supporting phase 3. The liver HRX215 phase 2b protocol compares liver-remnant growth at day 28 with placebo and includes postoperative liver failure among secondary outcomes. A 23 October 2026 conference abstract pools 61 rilparencel-treated kidney patients. Their estimated glomerular filtration rate, a measure of kidney filtration, declined at 1.78 mL/min/1.73 m²/year after first injection. This was an uncontrolled pooled analysis reported as a conference abstract.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b)–(c), phase 2 objectives and evidence preceding phase 3.

milestones.title: An organ-regeneration treatment establishes effectiveness in adequate and well-controlled studies.
milestones.criterion: An organ-regeneration treatment establishes effectiveness through two adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations, or one such investigation plus confirmatory evidence when FDA accepts that basis. Endpoints and safety assessment are indication-specific. For kidney rilparencel, PROACT 1 uses a confirmatory composite of ≥40% estimated filtration-rate loss, a rate <15 mL/min/1.73 m² sustained for 30 days and/or chronic dialysis or transplantation, or renal/cardiovascular death. ProKidney's 9 November 2026 filing describes ongoing phase 3 development.
milestones.set_by: FDA, August 2026 cellular and gene therapy development guidance, questions 32–34.
milestones.threshold_quote: two adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations to establish effectiveness

not_found: No shared numerical threshold for tissue regeneration, growth termination or follow-up was found in FDA, EMA or ISSCR guidance.
The delayed-miR-199a paper could not be opened at its institutional, publisher or PMC URLs.
The SALVADOR-HF ClinicalTrials.gov page exposed no protocol text.
The 2026 rilparencel trial paper could not be inspected through its publisher or PMC pages.

results.finding: In a phase I trial, 36 healthy men received the liver-regeneration candidate HRX215; no severe or serious adverse events were reported.
results.detail: The placebo-controlled trial included 12 additional healthy men and assessed safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics. It did not test liver regeneration in patients.
results.quote: To assess the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of HRX215, a placebo-controlled exploratory phase I first-in-human study (European Union Drug Regulating Authorities Clinical Trials [EudraCT] 2021–000193-28) was performed with 48 male healthy volunteers, allocated to six treatment groups

results.finding: One liver resection patient completed 28 days of darizmetinib in a phase 1b study.
results.detail: The release reports a favorable safety profile but does not state that the phase 1 protocol assesses pharmacological effects and dose-associated adverse effects.
results.quote: the first patient undergoing major liver resection due to liver metastases originating from colorectal cancer has completed the 28 day treatment with darizmetinib (formerly HRX215) in the second pilot part of its ongoing Phase 1b/2a study.

results.finding: In 24 patients receiving scheduled bilateral rilparencel, annual eGFR decline improved by 78% after treatment.
results.detail: The phase 2 trial assessed diabetic kidney disease and treatment-related risks. It compared post-treatment kidney function with historical pre-treatment data, without a placebo group; a sham-controlled phase 3 study was ongoing.
results.quote: Bilateral kidney injections with rilparencel was associated with a 78% improvement in the annual eGFR decline in kidney function.

results.finding: In phase 2 cirrhosis patients, sample size not stated, death or transplant occurred in 30.8% of macrophage-treated patients.
results.detail: The study reports a lower death-or-transplant risk than standard care and no evidence of increased serious adverse events attributable to therapy. Regeneration is supported by preclinical findings; the text does not demonstrate new liver tissue formation in patients or explicitly state support for phase 3.
results.quote: Macrophage-treated patients in MATCH01 phase 2 demonstrated a significantly lower risk of death or transplant within the LTFU period (30.8%) compared with standard medical care (58.3%); macrophage-treated patients had an additional 252 days of restricted mean survival time within the LTFU period.
